episode_title: The Shogun Who Sealed Japan for 200 Years: Tokugawa Iemitsu
youtube_title: One Shogun Sealed Japan for 200 Years — But He Left One Door Open
youtube_description:
This summer, in 1639, a shogun in his thirties will shut Japan's ports to a whole European nation — and yet leave one narrow door open. He was an heir nobody was sure of, a man who outlasted his own brother. Why would Tokugawa Iemitsu seal a country for more than 200 years? Follow time-travelling reporter Tokio Kamiya as he files a dispatch from Edo, 1639.

📰 Your reporter: Tokio Kamiya, a former Tokyo foreign correspondent. His grandfather's brass pocket watch carries him to one day of Japan's past at a time. He can watch and he can speak, but he can never change what happens. Every episode is his dispatch from the scene.

teaser_narration: Edo, 1639. I stand in a corridor as councillors carry out a sealed order. The Portuguese are to be shut out of Japan for good. The man who signed it was once an heir in doubt. Why close a country, and leave one door open?
shorts_narration: 1635. No Japanese may sail abroad. 1639. No Portuguese may land. One shogun, one signature, and a country shut for over two centuries. But he left one door open. This is Tokugawa Iemitsu.

I may speak. I may not change a thing. Today it sets me down in Edo, in the summer of 1639. In the great castle, the third Tokugawa shogun, Iemitsu, still in his thirties, is deciding who may sail into Japan. I have one day to learn why.

scenes.narration: Let me start with what is solid. I carry the records in my notebook. Iemitsu is born in 1604, the grandson of Ieyasu and the eldest surviving son of Hidetada, the future shogun. But the story goes that his mother favours his younger brother Kunimatsu, a quick, charming boy. The servants begin to take sides. Every meal, every gift, every bow becomes a small measurement of favour. The child who will rule Japan grows up knowing one thing: even his own family may not choose him.

scenes.narration: His nurse, a woman called Kasuga, refuses to accept it. The tale says she slips away to Sunpu to plead with the retired Ieyasu himself. I cannot confirm the journey. What is clear is that the elder boy is treated as heir, and later accounts credit the old shogun's wishes for it. Kasuga is the first person I read about in this story who understands that a succession is a political act, and she may have changed the course of a country.

scenes.narration: In 1623, at nineteen, Iemitsu is made shogun. His father Hidetada steps aside in name, yet keeps the reins until his death in 1632. Later accounts say that Iemitsu tells the assembled lords that, unlike his grandfather and father, he was born to rule, and that anyone who disagrees may go home and ready an army. I cannot give you the date or the exact words. In the story, no lord goes home. Obedience, not affection, becomes the currency of his reign.

scenes.narration: Then the family question is closed. In 1632 Hidetada dies. Not long after, Kunimatsu, now called Tadanaga, is stripped of his domain and confined, and in the winter of 1633 he dies by his own hand. Iemitsu has no father above him and no rival beside him. I write the dates down twice, because they sit so close together. Whatever he is about to do to Japan, he now does alone. I think a man in that position stops fearing his family, and starts fearing everyone else.

scenes.narration: Now he builds his throne. In 1632 a great lord of Kyushu, Kato Tadahiro, loses his domain, and every lord learns that even famous names can be removed. In 1634 the shogun rides to Kyoto at the head of an enormous train. In 1635 the rules for the lords are rewritten: the great outside lords must spend alternate years in Edo. I watch a country learn to obey by the calendar. Nobody needs to fight. The shogun does not defeat the lords. He schedules them.

scenes.narration: Now to the door, and I read the orders one by one. Ieyasu's government has already banned the Christian faith. Under Iemitsu, the orders come one after another. In 1633, ships may sail abroad only with a special permit. In 1635, no Japanese may go overseas, and anyone who comes back from abroad faces death. In 1636, the Portuguese traders are confined to a small man-made island in Nagasaki harbour called Dejima. Each order is short. Together they are a wall. To a ship's captain it may read as paperwork. To a family on the quay, it is a goodbye.

scenes.narration: Another turn of the watch, another single day. Nagasaki, that autumn, a stone quay at dawn. I sit with an old boatman, and I tell him I am a travelling merchant. His brother sailed to Siam years ago to trade. He cannot come home now, the boatman says. The order says anyone who returns will be put to death, so the brother stays, and the letters have stopped. He watches a Portuguese ship being sent away under the new order. I do not know about gods, he says. I know about my brother.

scenes.narration: To see why the shogun hardens, I turn to the winter of 1637. In Shimabara and on the Amakusa islands, farmers crushed by taxes and persecution of their faith rise in revolt, with a youth named Amakusa Shiro as their figurehead. They hold the old Hara Castle for months, and the first commander sent against them dies there. In the spring of 1638 it falls, and almost everyone inside is killed. I think Edo sees not a hunger revolt, but a faith it cannot control.

scenes.narration: Edo, summer 1639. I wait in a corridor of the castle as the senior councillors file out with a sealed order. The shogun has decided. From now on, Portuguese ships may not come to Japan at all. These are the people who brought the guns, the silk, and the priests. Nobody argues. By the afternoon the order will be on the road to Nagasaki. A guard looks at me, then looks away. It is not a war. It is a signature, and I watch a door close.

scenes.narration: But there is a catch, and it is why I keep writing in my notebook. In 1638 a Dutch ship, at the commander's request, fires its guns on Hara from the sea. The Dutch are Protestants who trade and do not preach, and they are allowed to stay, under watch. I check the notebook again. The shogun is not closing Japan to the world. He is closing it to anyone he cannot control, and keeping one narrow window that he can.

scenes.narration: The watch hums in my coat. I leaf through my notebook, because I know what follows. In 1640 a Portuguese delegation sails from Macao to beg for the trade back. Edo will not listen. Most of the delegation is executed, and a few are sent home to carry the message. I do not enjoy writing it down. After that, nobody can say the order is a bluff, in Nagasaki or in Lisbon. The shogun has made his point to every sea captain at once.

scenes.narration: The next page in my notebook surprises me. In 1641 the Dutch are moved to Dejima, the same island, under guard. They must send in a report of the world's news. Chinese merchants trade at Nagasaki, and other contacts survive through Korea, the Ryukyu islands and the Ainu lands. So Japan is never truly sealed. It is a house with four narrow doors, and the shogun holds every key. I think of it less as a wall than as a valve.

scenes.narration: Dusk in Edo. Along the main road, a lord's long procession trudges out of the city, heading home to his domain after his year in attendance. I walk beside the spearmen for a while and count them, then stop, because the count is not the point. They say a lord who pays for such journeys has little left to pay for rebellion. I think this is the other half of the closed country: a Japan held shut from the inside.

scenes.narration: The watch grows warm against my chest. My day is almost over. I read the last page of Iemitsu's records. In 1651 he falls ill and dies, still in his forties. He is buried at Nikko, beside his grandfather Ieyasu, whose shrine he had rebuilt in splendour. The man who closed the sea is said to have spent his last wish on staying close to the one who built his house. I wonder whom he thought of, at the end. I close the notebook gently.

scenes.narration: Reporter's note. Back in my own century, I stand in Nagasaki, where Dejima has been rebuilt from old records beside a city that has swallowed the water around it. I think the word is younger than the thing, and those who lived inside it never used it. Names arrive late. The walls arrive first.

scenes.narration: Reporter's note. A sealed country does not stop thinking. Through that small window, books on medicine and astronomy come into Japan, and scholars learn Dutch to read them. They call it Dutch learning. When American ships arrive in 1853, the country that opens is not ignorant of the world. It has been reading about it for more than a century. I think of that whenever I hear that Japan woke up in 1853. Closed, yes. Blind, never. History is rarely as sealed as its labels.

scenes.narration: That is all I can carry from the records: a grandson, a rival, a decree, and one door that stayed firmly shut for more than two centuries.
